Assignment: mozilla speeds firefox release schedule biweekly

Upstream source headline: Mozilla speeds Firefox release schedule to biweekly

Create original headline language. Do not copy, lightly edit, or preserve the upstream source headline.

Make the headline as attractive, vivid, specific, and useful as the admitted reporting allows.

Name the actual subject. A curiosity gap may delay a detail, never the topic or factual payoff.

Keep it under 120 characters.

ARTICLE BODY:

Mozilla has announced a transition to a two-week release schedule for Firefox Desktop and Android, set to commence in September 2026. According to [Mozilla speeds Firefox release schedule to biweekly](https://www.theregister.com/software/2026/07/17/mozilla-speeds-firefox-release-schedule-to-biweekly/5274423), the shift was communicated via a mailing list post by Sylvestre Ledru, the organization's director of engineering. This adjustment moves the browser away from its current four-week cadence. 

While the new schedule is visible in the organization's upcoming release calendar, the change does not apply to Extended Support Release (ESR) versions, which will maintain an annual cycle. Ledru noted that the transition functions as an experiment. The accelerated schedule does not imply that all development must conclude twice as quickly, as features may still take the time they require to bake. This is not the first time the organization has attempted a shift in velocity, as a similar move occurred over a decade ago. Other industry participants have implemented comparable changes, such as Google’s decision to move Chrome to a four-weekly release cycle in 2021.

## Operational Changes and Security Updates

Ahead of the transition, Firefox 153 is scheduled for release on July 21, 2026. This version will serve as the next ESR iteration, providing security updates for at least 15 months. The upcoming software introduces functional changes to PDF handling, including the ability to merge multiple documents through drag-and-drop actions in the sidebar and the insertion of images as new pages. Other additions include a QR code generator for offline sharing and support for the Qualified Website Authentication Certificates defined under the EU’s eIDAS legislation.

Extensions will lose local-file access by default in this version, a change that may impact tools like the Multithreaded Download Manager. Users retain the ability to grant such permissions on a per-extension basis. Further interface updates include a map-pin icon in the address bar when a tab utilizes location data, along with expanded support for typed commands to mute sound or access experimental features. These adjustments reflect a broader, incremental effort to manage the complexity of the browser environment as release intervals compress.
